facts.statement: Diandongosuchus lived during the Middle Triassic period in China.
facts.quote: known from the Middle Triassic of China

facts.statement: The type species Diandongosuchus fuyuanensis was named in 2012 from fossils found in the Zhuganpo Formation of Yunnan Province.
facts.quote: The type species Diandongosuchus fuyuanensis was named in 2012 from the Zhuganpo Formation of Yunnan Province

facts.statement: Diandongosuchus had a skull that was proportionally large, long, and pointed, featuring oval-shaped eye sockets, antorbital openings, and temporal openings.
facts.quote: The skull of Diandongosuchus is proportionally large for its size; it was long and pointed, with oval-shaped eye sockets, antorbital and temporal openings

facts.statement: Diandongosuchus possessed small overlapping osteoderms, or bony scutes, covering many of its vertebrae.
facts.quote: Small overlapping osteoderms (bony scutes) overlay many of the vertebrae

facts.statement: Fossil evidence suggests Diandongosuchus ate small vertebrates like fish, indicated by bones found near the hips likely representing stomach contents.
facts.quote: At the back of the trunk near the hips are bones belonging to small vertebrates such as fish - likely the stomach contents of the individual

facts.statement: The scapula of Diandongosuchus is longer and narrower than the scapula of the related species Qianosuchus.
facts.quote: The scapula of Diandongosuchus is longer and narrower than that of Qianosuchus

facts.statement: Later studies by Stocker et al. (2016, 2017) reclassified Diandongosuchus as the basalmost known phytosaur.
facts.quote: However, a subsequent study conducted by Stocker et al. (2016, 2017) indicated it to be the basalmost known phytosaur instead

facts.statement: Skull characteristics shared with phytosaurs in Diandongosuchus, such as jaw joint shapes, likely strengthened the skull and bite for hunting.
facts.quote: Other certain skull characteristics shared with phytosaurs seem to be associated with strengthening of the skull and its bite, likely an adaptation related to hunting

facts.statement: Diandongosuchus fossils were found in a Ladinian-age marine limestone formation.
facts.quote: Diandongosuchus was found in a Ladinian-age marine limestone formation

facts.statement: Researchers suggest Diandongosuchus may have had a lifestyle similar to modern saltwater crocodiles, living along coastlines without being fully marine.
facts.quote: Diandongosuchus may have had a similar lifestyle to modern marine crocodylians like the saltwater crocodile that live along coastlines yet are not fully marine

facts.statement: Diandongosuchus is classified under the unranked order Phytosauria.
facts.quote: unranked_ordo: Phytosauria

facts.statement: The binomial name for the type species is Diandongosuchus fuyuanensis.
facts.quote: binomial: Diandongosuchus fuyuanensis

facts.statement: The species is known from a nearly complete articulated skeleton (ZMNH M8770) that lacks most of the tail.
facts.quote: Diandongosuchus es conocido a partir de un esqueleto casi completo articulado, (ZMNH M8770) que carece de la mayor parte de la cola.

facts.statement: The total length of the holotype specimen is 97 centimeters, while the estimated body length of the living animal is about 155 centimeters.
facts.quote: La longitud total de ZMNH M8770 es de 97 centímetros y la longitud estimada corporal del animal en vida es de cerca de 155 cm.

facts.statement: The skull is pointed, featuring oval eye orbits and anteorbital and temporal openings.
facts.quote: El cráneo de Diandongosuchus es aguzado, con órbitas oculares ovales, y aberturas anteorbitales y temporales (fenestras).

facts.statement: Two rows of overlapping bony scutes run along the neck, back, and tail, with two osteoderms above each vertebra.
facts.quote: Dos filas corren a lo largo del cuello, la espalda y la cola con dos osteodermos encima de cada vértebra.

facts.statement: Small osteoderms also covered the bones of the limbs.
facts.quote: Pequeños osteodermos también cubrían los huesos de las extremidades.

facts.statement: The scapula is longer and narrower than that of the related species Qianosuchus.
facts.quote: La escápula de Diandongosuchus es larga y estrecha que la de Qianosuchus.

facts.statement: Bones of small vertebrates like fish found near the hips likely came from the stomach contents of the individual.
facts.quote: En la parte posterior del tronco cerca de las caderas hay huesos pertenecientes a pequeños vertebrados como peces - probablemente procedentes de los contenidos estomacales del individuo.

facts.statement: It is closely related to Qianosuchus, an aquatic pseudosuchian that is the second most basal member of Poposauroidea.
facts.quote: Este fue hallado como cercanamente relacionado con Qianosuchus, un pseudosuquio acuático que es el segundo miembro más basal de Poposauroidea.

facts.statement: However, Diandongosuchus does not show clear adaptations for a marine lifestyle.
facts.quote: Sin embargo, Diandongosuchus no muestra rasgos que sean adaptaciones clara a la vida en el mar.

facts.statement: It may have led a lifestyle similar to modern marine crocodilians like the saltwater crocodile, living along coastlines without being fully marine.
facts.quote: Diandongosuchus puede haber llevado un estilo de vida similar al de los actuales cocodrilos marinos como el cocodrilo de agua salada que vive a lo largo de las líneas costeras aun no siendo totalmente marino.

facts.statement: The fossil association likely represents environments along the northern coasts of the Tethys Sea.
facts.quote: Ambas incluyen reptiles marinos como talatosaurios y notosaurios y probablemente representan ambientes a lo largo de las costas septentrionales del mar de Tetis.

facts.statement: The genus is classified within the parent group Phytosauria.
facts.quote: Parent group: Phytosauria

facts.statement: The animal belongs to the class Reptilia.
facts.quote: Class: Reptilia

facts.statement: The type species of the genus is Diandongosuchus fuyuanensis.
facts.quote: Type species: Diandongosuchus fuyuanensis

facts.statement: The species lived during the Ladinian stage, between 241.464 and 237 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Ladinian to Ladinian (241.464 to 237 million years ago)
